articles.title: The Box Says I Was Drinking
articles.author: Daniel Bailey
articles.content_excerpt: SCRAM. Secure Continuous Remote Alcohol Monitoring. Eight ounces of Colorado engineering that spends its entire existence trying to prove you are the kind of man who cannot be trusted with a single night of ordinary work. The company calls it continuous alcohol monitoring. The men who bill me call it Wednesday. The court ordered it. It was not optional. I rent it from a private company for $66.50 a week, and the bill comes to me. Read more via Scalawag : The Box Says I Was Drinking .

articles.author: Ben Case
articles.content_excerpt: The blue tidal wave that swept congressional and local elections around the country is leaving a new political landscape in its wake. The generational scope of Democratic wins and unprecedented success of democratic socialist candidates notwithstanding, the president’s party almost always loses midterm elections, often by wide margins. How much do the election results reflect a shift in society’s politics, and how much do they reflect an extreme version of the standard two-party pendulum swing? And more importantly, where are the opportunities to push organizing to new horizons in this new terrain? articles.title: Capitalism Is More Than a Legal Regime
articles.author: E. Ahmet Tonak
articles.content_excerpt: “Capitalism is a legal regime, not just an economic system as conventional wisdom has it.” With this opening sentence, Katharina Pistor takes the argument of her previous book , The Code of Capital , a step further. There she showed how lawyers turn assets into capital through property, contract, collateral, trust, corporate, and bankruptcy law. Her new book extends the argument to capitalism as a whole. If law so thoroughly constitutes capitalism, she asks, why is it “so resistant to legal governance”? And how might we transform it? Pistor has much to say about the legal powers of capital, and her account deserves serious attention. Yet I find two fundamental problems with her argument. This low-profile Air Force Reserve chaplain is a clean-living Southern Baptist minister, small town lawyer, and former congressman from Georgia.
